The Malagasy rainbow frog (Scaphiophryne gottlebei) displays pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a trait common among microhylids that inhabit the karstic plateaus of western Madagascar. Adult females attain a significantly larger body size, with a maximum snout-vent length measured in a comprehensive field survey reaching 4 centimeters [Li = 4 centimeters], a dimension that reflects the selective pressures of fecundity in this explosive breeder. Males, in contrast, are considerably more diminutive, with the largest recorded individuals reaching only 3 centimeters [Li = 3 centimeters] in snout-vent length. This marked difference in ultimate body size is thought to be driven by the intense scramble competition observed in ephemeral breeding pools, where smaller male size may confer an advantage in maneuverability. The mass at hatching for this species is remarkably low; upon eclosion from its gelatinous egg mass, the newly emerged tadpole weighs just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value consistent with the production of numerous, small yolk-laden eggs. This initial wet weight at birth places the species at the lower end of the range seen in sympatric microhylids.

The timing of early life-history events in Scaphiophryne gottlebei is tightly coupled to the brief seasonal rains that inundate their canyon-floor breeding sites. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the interval from egg hatching to the completion of metamorphosis was recorded as 200 days after hatching , a remarkably protracted larval period for a frog of this body size. This extended duration spent as a tadpole is hypothesized to be an adaptation to the unpredictable availability of high-quality food resources within small temporary pools, where growth may be periodically arrested. By the time of metamorphic climax, the juveniles achieve a snout-vent length at metamorphosis of approximately 1.6 centimeters . The long developmental trajectory stands in stark contrast to that of many other microhylid species from similar latitudes, which often complete metamorphosis in under half that time. This slow growth strategy may also be linked to the relatively cool water temperatures found in their deep sandstone canyons.

Sexual maturation in males of this species is not a uniform process, with field and captive studies revealing considerable individual variation in the timing of puberty. A significant cohort of male individuals first exhibit secondary sexual characteristics and achieve reproductive viability at a snout-vent length of 3.7 centimeters [Lp = 3.7 centimeters]. However, other mature individuals within the same population become reproductively active at a considerably smaller body size, with puberty documented at 2.8 centimeters [Lp = 2.8 centimeters]. This bimodal pattern in the size at which male puberty occurs suggests that alternative reproductive tactics may be at play, potentially involving competitive interactions at the breeding aggregations. The existence of two distinct size thresholds for the onset of gonadal maturation is unusual among anurans and points to a flexible life-history strategy that allows males to exploit varying social and ecological conditions. The corresponding somatic growth during this period is substantial, as males must reach one of these two size milestones before initiating their first amplexus.

Adult body mass in Scaphiophryne gottlebei scales predictably with the pronounced sexual size dimorphism observed in snout-vent length. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown females has been estimated at 6.5 grams [Wwi = 6.5 grams], a mass that represents the maximum achieved under favorable foraging conditions. This substantial body mass is necessary to support the production of the large gelatinous egg clutches characteristic of the species. In contrast, adult males are significantly lighter, with a maximum recorded ultimate wet weight of 2.75 grams [Wwi = 2.75 grams], reflecting their considerably smaller frame. This difference of nearly 2.4 times in wet weight between the sexes is one of the most extreme examples of female-biased size dimorphism within the family Microhylidae. The lower mass of males likely reduces their energetic costs during the prolonged breeding season, allowing them to remain active in the breeding pools for extended periods while competing for access to gravid females.

At a mean water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the reproductive and life-history schedule of the Malagasy rainbow frog is accelerated relative to other amphibians of similar ultimate body size. Females achieve their maximum reproductive rate by producing an average of roughly 1.4 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 1.4 eggs per day], a capacity that is sustained throughout the short breeding window. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species under natural conditions is 730 days [am = 730 days], a relatively short total longevity that is typical of small-bodied, explosive-breeding anurans that experience high adult mortality during the dry season at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This compressed lifespan, combined with the long metamorphic duration of 200 days from hatching , implies that individuals have a restricted window for growth and reproduction at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. The species thus conforms to a high-risk, high-reward life-history strategy, where rapid investment in early reproduction is favored over extended somatic persistence in a challenging and seasonal environment.
